quickStart.keyIdea: Vue is a React-like way to build user interfaces, but it packages the common patterns into a more integrated framework centered on templates and built-in reactivity.
quickStart.quickSummary:
Vue belongs to the same family as React: both build interfaces from components, render declaratively, and keep data flowing one way. The main difference is that Vue’s default style leans on HTML-like templates and built-in reactivity, so state changes update the UI with less setup.

Vue is used for anything from small interactive widgets to full single-page apps. Its component model makes UI pieces reusable, while props and events handle parent-child communication. The comparison with React is useful, but it breaks where Vue’s template-first, more integrated framework style differs from React’s JSX and library-first ecosystem.

pages.title: 01 - Vue’s Core Identity and Architecture
pages.rawNotes: ## Vue’s core identity Vue is an open-source JavaScript framework for building user interfaces, and it was created by Evan You with a first public release in 2014. Vue’s main job is to help you connect application state to what users see, so your interface stays consistent as data changes. Vue is maintained by an open-source community led by the Vue core team, which supports ongoing improvements and ecosystem growth. ## Declarative rendering and reactivity Vue uses declarative rendering, which means you describe what the UI should look like for a given state rather than manually issuing DOM operations. Vue’s reactivity system tracks dependencies between state and the parts of the template that use it, and it triggers relevant updates when state changes. This creates a practical workflow where you update data and let Vue update the visible output efficiently. ## Components as reusable building blocks Vue interfaces are built from reusable, composable components, which lets you decompose a larger UI into smaller, independently understandable units. A component typically encapsulates structure, behavior, and presentation, so you can reuse it across different parts of an application. Vue commonly uses single-file components, where a single file includes a template section, a script section, and a style section. ## Progressive adoption and where Vue fits Vue supports progressive adoption, meaning you can start with isolated widgets and later expand toward complete applications. This flexibility is useful when you want to enhance server-rendered pages with embedded interactive areas, or when you want to organize a client-side single-page application. Vue can therefore fit different project sizes and integration styles without forcing an all-or-nothing rewrite. ## Minimal example: reactive greeting in a single-file component Here is a minimal Vue single-file component that displays a reactive greeting. ```vue ``` ## From widget to routed application A concrete progression is to begin with one component like the greeting widget, then add more components to build a page, and finally introduce routing so navigation swaps between views without reloading the whole page. Vue’s component model and reactivity make this step-by-step growth manageable. ## Framework, not language Vue is a framework rather than a programming language, runtime, or browser replacement, so you still write JavaScript and use Vue to structure and update the user interface.

pages.title: 02 - Templates, Reactivity, and Component Communication
03 - APIs, Tooling, and Vue Compared with React
pages.rawNotes: ## Vue APIs: Options API vs Composition API Vue gives you two ways to organize component logic, and choosing between them is mostly about how you want to structure code. The **Options API** groups logic into familiar options such as `data`, `methods`, and `computed`, which can feel approachable because related concerns are placed in recognizable sections. The **Composition API** groups related logic inside **setup-based functions** and **composables**, which helps when you want to keep behavior together, reuse it across components, or work comfortably with TypeScript. A practical way to think about it is that both APIs support the same overall goal, but they encourage different organization styles. If your component is small, the Options API can be straightforward, while larger components often benefit from the Composition API’s ability to group and reuse related behavior. ## Official tooling: Vite, Router, and Pinia For new Vue projects, the standard modern workflow commonly uses **Vite** as the build tool to scaffold and run the application. For navigation, **Vue Router** is the official routing solution for Vue applications. When you need shared application state across multiple parts of the app, **Pinia** is the officially recommended state-management library for new Vue projects. This tooling story matters because it reduces decision fatigue, letting you focus on building features rather than assembling core infrastructure. ## Vue vs React: same ideas, different expression Vue and React both use components, declarative updates, and one-way data flow, but they differ in how developers express UI. Vue commonly uses **HTML-like templates and directives**, while React commonly expresses markup through **JSX** and relies more on chosen libraries for many defaults. Vue is often described as a more integrated framework experience, whereas React is primarily a UI library. Neither approach is universally superior, because project constraints determine fit. ## Example: Composition API with a computed value ```vue ``` This example shows how the Composition API can keep state (`count`) and derived state (`doubleCount`) together, while the template declaratively renders the current values.

bridgeBlocks.title: Vue templates vs React JSX
bridgeBlocks.body: If you know React, Vue templates play a similar role to JSX: both describe UI from state and re-render when data changes. Vue’s `{{ }}` interpolation and directives like `v-bind` and `v-on` map to the same basic ideas as embedding expressions and attaching handlers in React. Caveat: Vue keeps more logic in the template syntax, while React usually puts more in JavaScript, so the code shape feels different.

quickStart.keyIdea: Photography is the craft of shaping light into a clear image, where exposure, focus, composition, and timing decide how the scene is recorded.
quickStart.quickSummary:
Photography is about controlling how light becomes a picture. Exposure balances aperture, shutter speed, and ISO, while focus and white balance help keep the subject sharp and the color believable.

Composition gives the frame purpose by guiding attention with placement, lines, and space. Lightroom can refine a strong capture, but it cannot fully rescue poor exposure or focus, so the camera decisions still matter most. The boundary is simple: editing improves a photo; it does not replace making one well.

pages.title: 01 - Exposure and Camera Controls
pages.rawNotes:
## What “exposure” really means
Exposure is the sensor’s received light, and it is determined by aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. These three controls work together, so you can often reach similar brightness with different trade-offs. Think of exposure as a balance you adjust to match the look you want and the motion you must capture.

## Aperture: light and depth of field
A wider aperture, shown by a smaller f-number, admits more light and reduces depth of field. A narrower aperture, shown by a larger f-number, admits less light and increases depth of field. This means aperture affects both how bright the image is and how much of the scene appears acceptably sharp.

## Shutter speed: motion and light
A faster shutter speed reduces motion blur but admits less light. A slower shutter speed admits more light, but it can record camera shake or subject movement. If your subject is moving, you typically need a faster shutter speed to keep details crisp.

## ISO: brightness, noise, and dynamic range
Raising ISO brightens the recorded image, but it generally increases noise and reduces dynamic range. Lower ISO usually preserves more tonal detail, especially in challenging lighting. When you raise ISO, you are trading cleanliness of the image for brightness.

## Exposure compensation and metering
Exposure compensation shifts the camera’s metered exposure when the scene is unusually bright or dark. Metering estimates exposure from scene brightness, but reflective snow, backlit subjects, or dark backgrounds can mislead it. In those cases, the camera may underexpose or overexpose unless you correct it.

## Reading the histogram to protect detail
The histogram shows tonal distribution, and clipped highlights or shadows contain lost detail. If the histogram indicates clipping, you should adjust exposure compensation or your manual settings to recover what you can. This is a practical way to confirm whether your exposure preserved useful tones.

## Example trade-offs you can compare
Try the same subject three times: use a wide aperture for a brighter frame with less depth of field, use a fast shutter speed for sharper motion with less light, and use high ISO for brightness with more noise. You will see that similar brightness can still produce different sharpness, blur, and texture.

## Lightroom histogram correction example
In Lightroom, start by checking the histogram for clipped highlights, then reduce exposure and use highlight adjustments to bring the clipped tones back into the visible range. After correction, compare the histogram again to confirm that the tonal distribution is no longer pushed into clipping.

pages.title: 02 - Focus, Color, and Light
pages.rawNotes:
## Focus: make the right detail sharp
Start by deciding what must be sharp in your scene, because focus is about placing sharpness where it matters most. In a portrait, that often means focusing on an eye so the viewer’s attention lands immediately. For stationary subjects, autofocus behavior can be simpler, but for continuously moving subjects you typically need autofocus modes that distinguish stationary from moving action.

When you want control over exactly what receives focus, use single-point autofocus so the camera focuses on the chosen subject detail rather than guessing. For moving subjects, focus placement and shutter timing work together, since the moment you press the shutter determines whether the subject is in the focus plane. A useful way to think about this is that autofocus selection and tracking behavior help you stay locked, while timing helps you capture the moment that is actually sharp.

## Depth of field: more than background blur
Depth of field describes the range that appears acceptably sharp, and it changes with aperture, focal length, subject distance, and sensor format. This means the same “background blur” look can come from different setups, so you should judge depth of field based on your framing and distance, not only on the background.

## Color: correct or intentionally preserve
Different light sources have different color temperatures, such as daylight, shade, and tungsten, and mixed lighting can add complexity. White balance compensates for these color temperature differences, which helps preserve accurate color when you want it, or it can be used to intentionally keep a certain mood.

## RAW vs JPEG: flexibility vs speed
RAW files preserve more adjustable tonal and color data than processed JPEG files, which makes RAW a strong choice when you expect to recover highlights or adjust color significantly. JPEG files are smaller and immediately viewable, but they rely on in-camera processing and compression, which reduces later flexibility.

## Light direction and quality: shape the scene
Before changing camera settings, observe light direction, size, and contrast. Front light tends to reveal detail evenly, side light emphasizes texture, and backlight can create silhouettes or rim light. Hard light creates stronger shadows and contrast than soft, diffused light, so the same subject can look dramatically different depending on how the light falls.

pages.title: 03 - Composition, Workflow, and Editing
pages.rawNotes:
## Composition first, then refine with editing.
Composition is the plan for how subjects, lines, shapes, space, and visual weight sit inside the frame, so your viewer instantly knows what matters. A helpful starting guide is the rule of thirds, which suggests placing important elements near grid intersections or lines, but it should not override what the scene is actually saying. Look for leading lines that pull attention toward a subject or focal area, and use negative space to isolate the subject and communicate scale, calm, or direction.

Before you shoot, inspect the edges and the background for clutter, and check whether empty space supports the message you want. If the background distracts, change your viewpoint by moving lower or higher, because that can alter relationships, scale, and what ends up behind your subject. Also remember that focal length changes the angle of view and how the frame feels, while camera position primarily changes perspective, so try moving your body before assuming the lens alone will fix the composition.

When you edit, use a non-destructive Lightroom workflow that preserves the original file while applying reversible edits and metadata. A practical flow is import, organize, select, develop, export, and back up, which keeps decisions traceable and reduces accidental loss. Start with profiles and global adjustments, then move to targeted corrections so you do not fight the image with overly specific changes too early.

Finally, apply finishing edits with restraint so they support the subject without creating distracting artifacts. Cropping can remove distractions, but it should not replace better framing decisions, and sharpening should be judged at viewing size so it looks crisp rather than crunchy. Export settings depend on where the image will go, since web delivery needs suitable dimensions and color handling, while prints require output-specific resolution and color management.

### Example: two viewpoints, one subject.
Imagine photographing the same person standing near a path, and try one composition from a low angle that uses the path’s edges as leading lines, then another from a higher angle that leaves more negative space above the head for calm separation.

### Example: a Lightroom workflow you can repeat.
Import the photos, organize them into a labeled set, select the best candidates, apply non-destructive edits in Develop, export a JPEG for web, and back up the catalog and files so the work remains recoverable.

bridgeBlocks.title: Focus before editing
bridgeBlocks.body: Lightroom can refine sharpness after capture, but it cannot truly fix a missed focus point. That makes focus a good in-camera decision first: choose the subject detail that must be sharp, then use editing only for small improvements like clarity or sharpening. This is similar to how Lightroom helps polish a photo rather than replace good technique. Caveat: heavy sharpening can create artifacts, so it is not the same as real optical focus.
